claims.text: A floating object is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the water it displaces (Archimedes' principle).

The same is true of steel ships.

claims.text: Initial stability is described by the metacentric height GM = KB + BM − KG: the centre of buoyancy, the metacentre and the centre of gravity, measured from the keel.

evidence.excerpt: GM = KB + BM - KG
For small heeling angles (<5 to 10 degrees):

claims.assumptions: Slide 10 gives BM = It/∇ for small angles and slide 15 gives It = LB³/12 for a rectangular waterplane (stacked formulas, not matchable as text; read on the PDF). For a box barge this gives BM = B²/(12T), used in analysis/design_model.py.
claims.intended_visual: Section: G, B and M marked on the platform; G rises when buildings are added
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no loads, stresses, motions, mooring forces or safety margins beyond quoted facts

claims.text: Moving a weight sideways on a floating body makes it list until the shifted centre of gravity is balanced: for small angles GM = w·d / (W·tan θ). A vessel can also be excessively stable.

evidence.excerpt: Take a vessel floating on the free surface and place a weight directly over the center of gravity. The ship will settle slightly deeper into the water but not roll.
where w is the mass of the weight (lbs), d is the distance (inches) the weight is moved, W is the displacement of the vessel (lbs) and tan θ is the tangent of the roll (list) angle.
Larger values can make a ship excessively stable.

claims.assumptions: Ship-design guidance; the film uses the relation, not the ship GM rule of thumb (3–5% of beam).
claims.intended_visual: A load moves to the platform edge; the platform tilts slightly (angle from analysis/design_model.py, labelled illustrative)
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no loads, stresses, motions, mooring forces or safety margins beyond quoted facts

claims.text: The metacentre idea holds only for small angles; beyond about 10 to 15 degrees of heel engineers need the full righting-arm (GZ) curve.

evidence.excerpt: The concept of the metacenter is only really valid for small angles of motion.
For large heeling angles (> 10 to 15 degrees)
Need of more accurate description: GZ curve

claims.intended_visual: Card: 'small angles only' caveat beside the GM diagram
claims.scope: qualitative; illustrative models; no loads, stresses, motions, mooring forces or safety margins beyond quoted facts

claims.text: A large metacentric height makes a vessel 'stiff' in roll, with a large righting moment for small roll angles; a small metacentric height lets it roll slowly.

evidence.excerpt: If the metacentric height is large, then the vessel is considered to be “stiff” in roll – indicating that there will be a large righting moment as a result of small roll angles. In contrast, if the metacentric height is small then the ship rolls slowly due to a smaller righting arm.

claims.assumptions: Owner review 2026-11-08: GM describes the righting moment at small heel angles; it does not say how a platform moves in waves. The film must not infer wave response ('it follows the water') from GM. It may say that a small tilt under a shifted load tells us little about motion in waves.
